title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 7: OTHER CONSTITUTIONAL BATTLES
keywords: a living testimonial of Philippine heritage
right to match the foreigner's offer
Iglesia ni Cristo v. Court of Appeals
American Bible Society v. City of Manila
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- a round-up of three further constitutional controversies in which CJP found himself writing separately: the 'Filipino First' policy in Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS, the censorship of religious television in Iglesia ni Cristo v. Court of Appeals, and the national ID system in Ople v. Torres

His dissent in Manila Prince Hotel: while agreeing that Article XII, Section 10 is self-executing and that the Manila Hotel is part of the national patrimony, he rejected the majority's grant to a losing Filipino bidder of the right to match the winning foreign bid as 'unadulterated judicial legislation' absent any implementing statute

His Separate Opinion in Iglesia ni Cristo: concurring that the MTRCB may review religious programs but insisting that the 'dangerous tendency' standard in Section 3-c of PD 1986 is martial-law vintage and must give way to the 'clear and present danger' rule, with the statute's own 'contemporary Philippine cultural values' serving as the standard for immorality and indecency

His Separate Opinion in Ople v. Torres: voting to strike down AO 308 on the narrow ground that a national identification system is beyond the President's power to establish without legislation, and leaving the privacy and freedom-of-thought questions for a future case once Congress acts
sub_topics: Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS, written by Justice Bellosillo, set the mechanism for enforcing the 'Filipino First' policy of Article XII, Section 10, par. 2 of the 1987 Constitution

The Court was unanimous that the preference clause is a mandatory, positive command needing no implementing law, that national patrimony covers cultural heritage as well as natural resources, and that the Manila Hotel -- 'a living testimonial of Philippine heritage' -- qualifies, so the sale of the government's 51 percent was state action
The real dispute was the degree of preference: the majority (echoed by Justice Padilla's concurrence) held that a losing qualified Filipino may match the highest foreign bid and win the auction

Justice Puno dissented that Article XII, Section 10 is 'pro-Filipino and not anti-alien,' so the preference arises only when the Filipino's bid ties the foreigner's -- and CJP joined him while filing his own dissent

CJP's three-point dissent: without an empowering statute the majority's reading is judicial legislation that 'makes bidding a ridiculous sham'; it invites reverse comity and retaliation that would marginalize Filipinos abroad; and preference should operate only when all bids are equal -- 'a victory for the qualified Filipino only when the scores are tied'

Iglesia ni Cristo v. Court of Appeals posed whether the review board (now the MTRCB) could screen and ban a religious television program said to attack other religions and to be indecent and contrary to law and good customs

The majority, through Justice Puno, read Section 3 of PD 1986 as covering all television programs including religious shows, holding religious freedom preferred but regulable on a clear-and-present-danger showing -- yet still allowed the banned 'Ang Iglesia ni Cristo' series to be broadcast

The dissenters -- Justices Melo, Padilla and Kapunan -- attacked administrative censorship as prior restraint, invoking Chief Justice Teehankee's grave-and-present-danger standard in American Bible Society v. City of Manila and arguing that violations are for courts, not an executive agency, to determine

Justice Kapunan faulted the majority's reliance on Sotto v. Ruiz for shifting to the producer the burden of showing that speech is protected, when any act restraining speech is presumed invalid; Justice Mendoza limited permissible censorship to 'a narrow class of cases involving pornography, excessive violence, and danger to national security'

CJP's Separate Opinion concurred in granting the petition but urged that the MTRCB act 'according to a standard and/or a limit': strike down 'with a dangerous tendency' as martial-law vintage, use 'clear and present danger' for incitement to violence or crime, and use the statutory standard of 'contemporary Philippine cultural values' for immorality and indecency

His catalogue of Filipino core values -- galang, pagbabahala, pananagutan, balikatan, malasakit, hiya, delikadesa, awa, tiwala, maka-Diyos, maka-tao -- and his examples of the 'Children of God' free-sex proselytizing and satanic blood sacrifices to show that religion cannot be governed by laissez faire
Justice Vitug's summation for the majority that regulation is not anathema to a right and that 'a delay is not too high a price to pay' for avoiding incalculable and lasting damage

The right to privacy: Time magazine's October 13, 1997 cover tolling 'the death of privacy,' and the daily invasions by credit cards, e-mail, ATMs, surveillance cameras, scanners, hospital and police records and commercial satellites

Ople v. Torres invalidated President Ramos' AO 308 creating a National Computerized Identification Reference System; Justice Puno grounded privacy in the Constitution, the Civil Code, RA 4200, RA 1405 and RA 8293, found no compelling state interest, and called the data reservoir 'a covert invitation to misuse'
Justices Mendoza and Kapunan dissented that AO 308 merely reused data already given under CA 591, RA 4136 and RA 8239, and afforded no basis for 'instruments of thought control'

CJP concurred only on the ground that the subject matter of AO 308 was beyond presidential power absent legislation, so the privacy and freedom-of-thought issues would ripen only after Congress acts -- a position Justice Davide joined, leaving the ponencia with just four unqualified votes out of the 8-6 majority

stances.claim: Absent a statute defining the degree of preference, the constitutional 'Filipino First' policy permits a qualified Filipino to prevail only when the bids are equal; letting a losing Filipino match and defeat the highest foreign bid is judicial legislation that turns bidding into a sham and invites retaliation against Filipino enterprises abroad.
stances.rhetorical_move: separation-of-powers objection plus consequentialist warning: no empowering law means no such remedy, and the reciprocity costs would fall on Filipinos in the global marketplace

stances.claim: The MTRCB may review religious programs, but it cannot act absolutely or whimsically: the 'dangerous tendency' standard of PD 1986 is martial-law vintage and should be struck down in favor of 'clear and present danger' for incitement, while the statute's own 'contemporary Philippine cultural values' supplies the standard for immorality and indecency.
stances.rhetorical_move: standard-supplying concurrence: accepting the power but confining it by locating a workable test inside the statute itself

stances.claim: AO 308 had to fall because a national identification system is beyond the President's power to establish without a legislative enactment; whether such a system infringes privacy or freedom of thought is not yet justiciable and should await a law from Congress.
stances.rhetorical_move: narrow-ground adjudication: deciding on the least constitutional footing and deferring the larger rights question as unripe

stances.claim: The national ID system would place the people's right to privacy in clear and present danger, since the vast reservoir of personal information is 'a covert invitation to misuse.'
stances.rhetorical_move: reporting the ponencia's rationale, which CJP declined to adopt as his own ground

notable_anecdotes: CJP closes his Manila Prince Hotel dissent with a schoolroom moral -- 'Do not do unto others what you do not want others to do unto you' -- and with the mordant aside 'Only in the Philippines!' about a bidding no Filipino can lose.

In his Iglesia ni Cristo opinion he pauses for 'just a word edgewise about cultural values,' reciting galang, pananagutan, malasakit, hiya, delikadesa, awa and maka-Diyos as what 'define us as a people, as Filipinos.'

He illustrates the limits of religious expression with the 'Children of God' who 'blew into town' and practised 'flirty-fishing' (free sex), asking how many would sit on their hands if such groups telecast programs for 'OUR children to watch.'

He opens the privacy section with Time magazine's October 13, 1997 cover tolling 'the death of privacy,' cataloguing credit cards, e-mail, ATM machines, surveillance cameras and supermarket scanners as daily invasions.

He notes the arithmetic of Ople v. Torres: eight votes to grant and six against, but only four justices gave unqualified agreement to Justice Puno's ponencia, with Justice Davide joining CJP's narrower legislative-power ground.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' gathers three further constitutional controversies in which Justice Panganiban wrote separately. In Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS, written by Justice Bellosillo, the Court unanimously held that the 'Filipino First' clause of Article XII, Section 10 is a mandatory, positive command needing no implementing law, that national patrimony embraces cultural heritage, and that the Manila Hotel -- 'a living testimonial of Philippine heritage' -- was covered, making the sale of the government's 51 percent a state action. The division came over the degree of preference: the majority and Justice Padilla would let a losing qualified Filipino match the highest foreign bid and win, while Justice Puno dissented that the clause is 'pro-Filipino and not anti-alien' and gives preference only on a tie. CJP joined Puno and added his own dissent, arguing that with no statute empowering a losing bidder to raise his bid, the majority's reading was 'unadulterated judicial legislation' that 'makes bidding a ridiculous sham,' invited reverse comity and retaliation abroad, and should be confined to equal bids -- 'a victory for the qualified Filipino only when the scores are tied.' In Iglesia ni Cristo v. Court of Appeals, the majority through Justice Puno upheld the MTRCB's power to screen religious programs while still allowing the banned series to air; Justices Melo, Padilla, Kapunan and Mendoza attacked administrative censorship as prior restraint, invoking Chief Justice Teehankee's standard in American Bible Society. CJP concurred in granting the petition but insisted the Board act 'according to a standard and/or a limit,' urging that the martial-law-vintage 'dangerous tendency' test be struck down in favor of 'clear and present danger,' and that the statute's own 'contemporary Philippine cultural values' govern questions of immorality and indecency -- illustrating the point with Filipino core values and with the 'Children of God' free-sex example. Finally, in Ople v. Torres, the Court voided President Ramos' AO 308 creating a national identification system; CJP voted to grant the petition only because the subject was 'beyond the powers of the President to regulate without a legislative enactment,' leaving the privacy and freedom-of-thought questions to ripen if and when Congress legislates.
